passages.text: Multiplexed Integrating Plasmids for Engineering of the Erythromycin Gene Cluster for Expression in Streptomyces spp. and Combinatorial Biosynthesis

Bacteria in the genus Streptomyces and its close relatives are prolific producers of secondary metabolites with antibiotic activity. <sentence_start/>Genome sequencing of these bacteria has revealed a rich source of potentially new antibiotic pathways, whose products have never been observed. <sentence_start/>Moreover, these new pathways can provide novel genes that could be used in combinatorial biosynthesis approaches to generate unnatural analogues of existing antibiotics. <sentence_start/>We explore here the use of multiple orthologous integrating plasmid systems, based on the <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> loci from phages TG1, SV1, and ϕBT1, to express the polyketide synthase (PKS) for erythromycin in a heterologous Streptomyces host. <sentence_start/>Streptomyces strains containing the three polyketide synthase genes <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> expressed from three different integrated plasmids produced the aglycone intermediate, 6-deoxyerythronolide B (6-dEB). <sentence_start/>A further pair of integrating plasmids, both derived from the ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> locus, were constructed carrying a gene cassette for glycosylation of the aglycone intermediates, with or without the tailoring gene, <italic toggle="yes">eryF</italic>, required for the synthesis of erythronolide B (EB). <sentence_start/>Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry of the metabolites indicated the production of angolosaminyl-6-dEB and angolosaminyl-EB. <sentence_start/>The advantages of using multiplexed integrating plasmids for engineering expression and for combinatorial biosynthesis were demonstrated.
INTRODUCTION

Actinobacteria, such as those in the genus Streptomyces and its close relatives, are rich sources of antibiotics and other bioactive compounds. <sentence_start/>Indeed, 70% of antibiotics in current use are derived from or inspired by secondary metabolites from these bacteria. <sentence_start/>In order to meet the growing need for new antibiotics, researchers are turning to new ways of bioprospecting (<citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2217/fmb.10.119" pmid="21073314" count="1">1</citation>, <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/1751-7915.12123" pmid="24661414" pmcid="PMC3992017" count="1">2</citation>). <sentence_start/>A promising approach is to exploit the multiple “silent” secondary metabolism pathways within actinobacterial genomes, to “wake up” the pathway and identify a new natural product. <sentence_start/>Genes from these new pathways can also be used in combinatorial biosynthetic approaches with known pathways to generate novel compounds (<citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrmicro2478" pmid="21189477" count="1">3</citation>). <sentence_start/>While cloning entire secondary metabolic pathways into heterologous hosts is now generally feasible (<citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/c3np70034h" pmid="23832108" count="1">4</citation>, <citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.1319584111" pmid="24449899" pmcid="PMC3918841" count="1">5</citation>), the tools that facilitate combinatorial biosynthesis and synthetic biology approaches are less well developed.

Phage-encoded integrases have been widely used in integrating vectors for gene cloning in the actinobacteria and especially in Streptomyces (<citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s10295-011-1069-6" pmid="22160317" count="1">6</citation>, <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jmb.2014.05.014" pmid="24857859" pmcid="PMC4111918" count="1">7</citation>). <sentence_start/>The vectors are convenient to use since they are easily maintained and genetically modified in Escherichia coli and can then be transferred by conjugation to Streptomyces, where they integrate into the chromosome at high efficiency. <sentence_start/>The plasmid size for transfer to Streptomyces appears to be limited more by their stability and maintenance in the E. coli donor strain rather than the ability to establish and integrate in the Streptomyces chromosome. <sentence_start/>The advantage of using integrating plasmids includes the stability conferred by the directionality of phage-encoded integrases (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/microbiolspec.MDNA3-0059-2014" pmid="26350324" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>The integration reaction involves a single DNA crossover between the phage attachment site, <italic toggle="yes">attP</italic> and the bacterial attachment site, <italic toggle="yes">attB</italic>, to generate the integrated DNA flanked by the recombinant sites, <italic toggle="yes">attL</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">attR</italic>. <sentence_start/>As the excision reaction, in which <italic toggle="yes">attL</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">attR</italic> recombine to regenerate <italic toggle="yes">attB</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">attP</italic>, can only occur in the presence of the recombination directionality factor (RDF), plasmid vectors based solely on the <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> locus remain stably integrated (<citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-2958.2011.07696.x" pmid="21564337" count="1">9</citation>). <sentence_start/>Another major advantage of using integrating plasmids is that they can be multiplexed without interference during recombination or conjugation and without any loss of stability, as shown previously by the introduction of ϕC31 and ϕBT1 based plasmids into S. coelicolor and S. lividans (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/JB.185.17.5320-5323.2003" pmid="12923110" pmcid="PMC180994" count="1">10</citation>). <sentence_start/>Recently, two more phage-encoded <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> loci, from TG1 and SV1, have been described for use in integrating plasmids into Streptomyces genomes (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1472-6750-14-51" pmid="24885867" pmcid="PMC4068962" count="1">11</citation>, <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1574-6968.2009.01683.x" pmid="19624407" count="1">12</citation>). <sentence_start/>These four orthologous integration loci potentially provide a means for efficient combinatorial engineering of antibiotic pathways.

To exemplify the use of multiplexed integrating vectors to facilitate genetic manipulation and combinatorial biosynthesis of antibiotic pathways, we chose the erythromycin biosynthesis cluster (Fig. 1A). <sentence_start/>Erythromycin A is a bacteriostatic macrolide antibiotic produced from Saccharopolyspora erythraea (formerly Streptomyces erythreus) (<citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" pmid="24336183" doi="10.1038/nrmicro3155" count="1">13</citation>). <sentence_start/>The biosynthesis of erythromycin can be divided into two stages (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/cr9600316" pmid="11851474" count="1">14</citation>). <sentence_start/>First, the modular polyketide synthase (PKS) complex, 6-deoxyerythronolide B (6-dEB) synthase, catalyzes the sequential condensation of proprionyl-coenzyme A (CoA) and six methylmalonyl-CoA precursors to generate 6-dEB, the first isolatable intermediate in the pathway (Fig. 1). <sentence_start/>The second stage is the conversion of 6-dEB to erythromycin A, starting with the conversion of 6-dEB to erythronolide B (EB) by EryF hydroxylase (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/bi00059a004" pmid="8448148" count="1">15</citation>). <sentence_start/>Two deoxysugars are then transferred to the aglycone ring to generate the first bioactive intermediate, erythromycin D (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/bi00059a004" pmid="8448148" count="1">15</citation>); EryBV glycosyltransferase transfers <sc>l</sc>-mycarose to yield 3-<italic toggle="yes">O</italic>-mycarosylerythronolide B and then EryCIII, activated by EryCII, transfers <sc>d</sc>-deoxydesosamine to the C-5 hydroxyl (<citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/cr9600316" pmid="11851474" count="1">14</citation>, <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9353926" doi="10.1099/00221287-143-10-3251" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>The genes required for the biosynthesis of the activated sugars, TDP-deoxymycarose and TDP-deoxydesosamine, are all encoded within the erythromycin gene cluster (<citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9353926" doi="10.1099/00221287-143-10-3251" count="1">16</citation>). <sentence_start/>The final two tailoring steps, hydroxylation of C-12 by EryK hydroxylase (<citation rid="B17" ref-type="bibr" pmid="8416893" doi="10.1128/jb.175.1.182-189.1993" pmcid="PMC196112" count="1">17</citation>), and methylation the 3′-OH of mycarose by EryG methyltransferase lead to the final product erythromycin A (<citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF00290659" pmid="1840640" count="1">18</citation>) (Fig. 1).
FIG 1

Overview of the biosynthesis of erythromycin. <sentence_start/>(A) Map of the erythromycin gene cluster from S. erythraea NRRL 2338. <sentence_start/>(B) Synthesis of erythromycin A showing the intermediates 6-deoxyerythronolide B (6-dEB) and erythronolide B (EB). <sentence_start/>(C) Four activated sugars relevant to the present study.

The biosynthetic pathway of erythromycin A offers multiple opportunities for combinatorial biosynthesis and the production of unnatural analogues. <sentence_start/>Genetic manipulation of such a large cluster comprising 55 kbp and 22 genes represents a daunting challenge (Fig. 1) (<citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt1297" pmid="17369815" count="1">19</citation>). <sentence_start/>Engineering the erythromycin gene cluster in the native strain presents further difficulties due to the fastidious nature of S. erythraea and the low frequency of transformation by large plasmids (<citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.chembiol.2010.09.013" pmid="21095573" count="1">20</citation>). <sentence_start/>Despite these, previous researchers have been immensely successful at rational alteration of the pathway to produce new analogues of the intermediate 6-dEB (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.8036492" pmid="8036492" count="1">21</citation><citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B22" doi="10.1016/S1074-5521(96)90069-1" pmid="8939702" count="1">-</citation><citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.7770773" pmid="7770773" count="1">23</citation>). <sentence_start/>Several of these studies have relied on expression in a heterologous host, S. coelicolor, S. lividans, or E. coli (<citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/MMBR.65.1.106-118.2001" pmid="11238987" pmcid="PMC99020" count="1">24</citation>). <sentence_start/>Using a freely replicating SCP2*-derived plasmid encoding all three of the PKS enzymes (DEBS1, DEBS2, and DEBS3, encoded by <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic>), Kao et al. was able to express 6-dEB and 8,8a-deoxyoleandolide in S. coelicolor (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.8036492" pmid="8036492" count="1">21</citation>). <sentence_start/>Further work by McDaniel et al., using the same genetic construct as used by Kao et al., demonstrated that the aglycone ring could be modified by substitution of enzyme domains from the homologous rapamycin pathway to produce 61 6-dEB analogues (<citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.96.5.1846" pmid="10051557" pmcid="PMC26699" count="1">25</citation>). <sentence_start/>At the same time, Xue et al. placed the three <italic toggle="yes">eryA</italic> genes on different plasmids using SCP2* for <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic> and the ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> site for <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.96.21.11740" pmid="10518520" pmcid="PMC18356" count="1">26</citation>). <sentence_start/>Since two of the plasmids are derived using the same replicon, SCP2*, selection had to be constantly applied to ensure against plasmid loss (<citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.96.21.11740" pmid="10518520" pmcid="PMC18356" count="1">26</citation>). <sentence_start/>Despite this and other potential problems that were predicted to arise through the use of vectors derived from the same incompatibility group Xue et al. demonstrated the principle of in <italic toggle="yes">trans</italic> expression of the PKS genes in the heterologous host. <sentence_start/>Moreover, placing the three <italic toggle="yes">eryA</italic> genes on different plasmids greatly facilitated combinatorial engineering of the <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> genes.

Here, we adapt and improve the strategy taken by Xue et al., and we show that expression of the <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> genes can be achieved from three orthologous integrating vectors in S. coelicolor. <sentence_start/>Using a fourth plasmid, we demonstrate how the tailoring steps downstream of the synthesis of 6d-EB and EB might be easily modified.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Bacterial strains and culture conditions.

E. coli strain DH5α, E. coli strain ET12567(pUZ8002), and E. coli strain BW25113(pIJ790) were grown as described elsewhere (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>, <citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" count="1">28</citation>). <sentence_start/>E. coli strain DH5α was used for plasmid propagation and subcloning while E. coli strain BW25113(pIJ790) was used for recombineering using the REDIRECT method (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>). <sentence_start/>The DNA methylation deficient strain of E. coli, ET12567(pUZ8002) was used as the donor host for plasmid conjugation to Streptomyces species as described previously (<citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" pmid="3056907" doi="10.1128/jb.170.12.5607-5612.1988" pmcid="PMC211658" count="1">29</citation>).

Streptomyces strains were maintained on Soya Mannitol (SM) agar at 30°C (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" count="1">30</citation>). <sentence_start/>Streptomyces strains used as heterologous expression hosts were Streptomyces coelicolor J1929, a Δ<italic toggle="yes">pglY</italic> derivative of the wild-type strain M145 (<citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7642495" doi="10.1128/jb.177.16.4681-4689.1995" pmcid="PMC177233" count="1">31</citation>), Streptomyces coelicolor M512 (Δ<italic toggle="yes">redD ΔactII-orf4</italic> SCP1<sup>−</sup> SCP2<sup>−</sup>) (<citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1365-2958.1996.6491364.x" pmid="8858592" count="1">32</citation>), Streptomyces coelicolor M1152 [Δ<italic toggle="yes">act</italic> Δ<italic toggle="yes">red</italic> Δ<italic toggle="yes">cpk</italic> Δ<italic toggle="yes">cda rpoB</italic>(<italic toggle="yes">C1298T</italic>)], Streptomyces coelicolor M1154 (Δ<italic toggle="yes">act</italic> Δ<italic toggle="yes">red</italic> Δ<italic toggle="yes">cpk</italic> Δ<italic toggle="yes">cda rpoB</italic>(<italic toggle="yes">C1298T</italic>)], <italic toggle="yes">rpsL</italic>(<italic toggle="yes">A262G</italic>) (<citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1751-7915.2010.00219.x" pmid="21342466" pmcid="PMC3818861" count="1">33</citation>), and Streptomyces lividans TK24 (<italic toggle="yes">str-6</italic> SLP2<sup>−</sup> SLP3<sup>−</sup>) (<citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" count="1">30</citation>). <sentence_start/>Micrococcus luteus (Fleming strain) was grown in tryptic soy broth (TSB) at 30°C and was used as a challenge organism for the detection of antibiotic activity.
DNA manipulations.

Chemically competent E. coli cells were prepared, stored, and used in the transformation procedure as described previously (<citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" count="1">28</citation>). <sentence_start/>Plasmid DNA extraction from E. coli was performed using QIAprep spin miniprep kit according to the protocol supplied by the manufacturer (Qiagen). <sentence_start/>Restriction enzymes used during the study were obtained from New England BioLabs (NEB), and the digestion procedure was carried out according to the manufacturer's instructions. <sentence_start/>Phusion high-fidelity DNA polymerase (NEB) was used for PCR amplification unless otherwise stated. <sentence_start/>The primers used in the present study are listed in Table 1. <sentence_start/>Overlap extension PCR was used to attach two or more DNA fragments when required, as described previously (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15038153" doi="10.2144/04363BM04" count="1">34</citation>). <sentence_start/>An In-Fusion HD cloning kit (Clontech) was used generally for cloning DNA fragments according to the protocol supplied by the manufacturer.
Plasmid constructions. <sentence_start/>(i) Construction of pRF10.

The <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> region of the phage TG1 was amplified by PCR using TG1 genomic DNA as a template and the primer MS403. <sentence_start/>The amplified product fragment was then digested using SpeI and SphI and ligated using NEB quick ligation kit to the SphI/SpeI 1,994-bp fragment from pMS82 to generate pRF10. <sentence_start/>The ligation mixture was introduced into E. coli by transformation and used in a conjugation assay to verify efficient integration of pRF10 into S. coelicolor, S. lividans, S. venezuelae, S. avermitilis, and S. albus.
(ii) Construction of the expression plasmid pBF20.

pBF20 (Fig. 2) is an integrating plasmid derived from phage TG1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> and contains the <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic> gene under the control of the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter and the apramycin-resistant gene (<italic toggle="yes">aac(3)IV</italic>) for selection. <sentence_start/>pBF20 is a derivative of pIB023 (see Fig. S1 in the supplemental material), a plasmid containing the <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> genome region from the native erythromycin cluster. <sentence_start/>pIB023 was created by insertion of pCJR65 into the S. erythraea genome, followed by rescue the large EcoRI fragment containing all of the <italic toggle="yes">eryA</italic> genes (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0378-1119(98)00327-8" pmid="9714812" count="1">35</citation>). <sentence_start/>Upstream of <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic> in pIB023 is the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter and the <italic toggle="yes">actII-orf4</italic> gene encoding the activator of <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p (<citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0378-1119(98)00327-8" pmid="9714812" count="1">35</citation>). <sentence_start/>The recombineering procedure of Gust et al. (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>) was used to replace all of the DNA from the 3′ end of <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic> to the 3′ end of <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> in pIB023 with an overlap extension PCR product encoding <italic toggle="yes">aac(3)IV-oriT</italic>-TG1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> (<citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" pmid="15038153" doi="10.2144/04363BM04" count="1">34</citation>) generated from two PCR products. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">aac(3)IV-oriT</italic> disruption cassette was amplified by PCR using pIJ773 as the template and primers PBF20A-for and PBF20A-rev. <sentence_start/>The TG1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> locus was amplified using plasmid pRF10 with the primers PBF20B-for and PBF20B-rev. <sentence_start/>The primers PBF20A-for and PBF20B-rev were then used to create a single amplified product of 3,529 bp.

Plasmid constructs for the expression of 6dEB and the angolomycin glycosylation gene cassette.

Primers PBF20A-for and PBF20B-rev contained 39 nucleotides (nt) of sequence that were identical to the endpoints of the DNA to be retained in pIB023 and were necessary to mediate recombineering between the <italic toggle="yes">aac(3)IV-oriT</italic>-TG1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> PCR overlap extension product and pIB023 to remove the <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> genes. <sentence_start/>Recombineering was performed by electroporation of the 3,529-bp PCR fragment into E. coli strain BW25113(pIJ790, pIB023) after induction of the <italic toggle="yes">gam</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">red</italic>α, and <italic toggle="yes">red</italic>β genes by arabinose (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>). <sentence_start/>Selection for apramycin resistance yielded the desired plasmid, pBF20 (Fig. 2), which was confirmed by restriction analysis and nucleotide sequencing.
(iii) Construction of the expression plasmid pBF22.

pBF22 is an SV1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>-based integrating plasmid (<citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1472-6750-14-51" pmid="24885867" pmcid="PMC4068962" count="1">11</citation>) containing the <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> gene under the control of <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter and encodes the kanamycin-resistant gene (<italic toggle="yes">aphII</italic>) for selection (Fig. 2). <sentence_start/>To generate pBF22, pIB023 was digested with BglII and PacI, and the 13,582-bp DNA fragment was purified. <sentence_start/>This DNA fragment contains a 5′ truncated <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> gene downstream of the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic> promoter, the thiostrepton resistance gene (<italic toggle="yes">tsr</italic>), the ampicillin resistance gene (<italic toggle="yes">bla</italic>), and the E. coli colE1 plasmid origin of replication. <sentence_start/>The 390-bp region encoding the 5′ end of the <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> gene was amplified by PCR using pIB023 as a template and the primers PBF22A-for and PBF22A-rev and digested with BglII and PacI. <sentence_start/>The 13,582-bp fragment and the 390-bp fragments were ligated together to form plasmid pBF22a. <sentence_start/>The SV1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> locus was amplified by PCR using pBF3 and the primers PBF22B-for and PBF22B-rev and inserted by In-Fusion cloning into pBF22a cut with XbaI to give plasmid pBF22b. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">aphII</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> fragments were amplified separately by using the primer pairs PBF22C-for/PBF22C-rev and PBF22D-for/PBF22D-rev, respectively, and the templates pNRT4 (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/JB.185.17.5320-5323.2003" pmid="12923110" pmcid="PMC180994" count="1">10</citation>) and pIJ778 (<citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" count="1">27</citation>), respectively. <sentence_start/>Overlap extension PCR was then used with the primers PBF22D-for and PBF22C-rev to fuse the <italic toggle="yes">aphII</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> PCR fragments to generate a 1,259-bp fragment, which was inserted by In-Fusion cloning into pBF22b linearized with SphI. <sentence_start/>The final plasmid, pBF22, was confirmed by restriction analysis and nucleotide sequencing.
(iv) Construction of the expression plasmid pBF24.

pBF24 is ϕBT1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>-based integrating plasmid (<citation rid="B10" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/JB.185.17.5320-5323.2003" pmid="12923110" pmcid="PMC180994" count="1">10</citation>) harboring the <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic> gene downstream of the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter and containing <italic toggle="yes">ermE</italic> for selection (Fig. 2).

pBF24 was created in multiple steps. <sentence_start/>A 4,079-bp fragment encoding the 5′ part of <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic> was amplified using pIB023 as a template and the primers PBF24A-for and PBF24A-rev introducing a HpaI restriction site at the 3′ end (PBF24A-rev). <sentence_start/>A 4,475-bp fragment encoding the plasmid vector sequence (containing <italic toggle="yes">bla</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tsr</italic>, the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter, <italic toggle="yes">actII-orf4</italic>, and the <italic toggle="yes">colE1</italic> origin) was also amplified from pIB023 using the primers PBF24B-for and PBF24B-rev. <sentence_start/>The 4,079- and 4,475-bp fragments were then ligated together by infusion to generate pBF24A. The remaining 3′ part of the <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic> gene was amplified by using the primers PBF24C-for and PBF24C-rev and ligated with pBF24A cut with HpaI to form plasmid pBF24B. pBF24C was constructed by amplification of the <italic toggle="yes">ermE</italic> gene from S. erythraea BIOT-4480 using the primers PBF24D-for and PBF24D-rev and inserting it by In-Fusion cloning into pBF24B cut with XbaI. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> (amplified using the template pIJ773 and the primers PBF24E-for and PBF24E-rev) and the ϕBT1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> (amplified using pMS82 as the template and primers PBF24F-for and PBF24F-rev) loci were joined to generate a 2,312-bp fragment by overlap extension PCR, which was inserted by In-Fusion cloning into pBF24C cut with SbfI. <sentence_start/>The final plasmid, pBF24, was confirmed by restriction analysis and nucleotide sequencing.
(v) Construction of the expression plasmids pBF21, pBF23, and pBF25.

Alternative versions of pBF20, pBF22, and pBF24 (Fig. 2), called, respectively, pBF21, pBF23, and pBF25 were made in which the <italic toggle="yes">actII-orf4</italic>/<italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter was replaced with the native promoter <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>p (see Fig. S2 in the supplemental material).

To construct pBF21, pBF20 was digested with ClaI to yield three DNA fragments of 14,860, 3,521, and 156 bp. <sentence_start/>An overlap extension PCR product was generated from three PCR products: a 2,381-bp fragment containing the 5′ end of the <italic toggle="yes">tsr</italic> gene, the ColE1 origin, and the <italic toggle="yes">bla</italic> gene; a 240-bp fragment <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>p (amplified from the S. erythraea BIOT-0666 genomic DNA using the primers PBF21A-for and PBF21A-rev); and a 154-bp fragment containing the 5′ end of the <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic> gene that was lost after cutting with ClaI. <sentence_start/>The resulting fragment (2,715 bp, obtained using the primers PBF21C-for and PBF21B-rev) was inserted by In-Fusion cloning into the purified 14,860-bp ClaI fragment to generate pBF21.

For the pBF23, and pBF25 constructions, <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>p was amplified from the S. erythraea BIOT-0666 genomic DNA by primers PBF23-for/PBF23-rev and PBF25-for/PBF25-rev, respectively. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>p fragments were then inserted into pBF22 and pBF24, cut with SpeI/PacI and PacI/SspI, respectively. <sentence_start/>The new plasmids were verified by restriction analysis and sequencing.
(vi) Construction of the expression plasmid pBF27N.

pBF27N is an integrating plasmid encoding the ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>, derived from a plasmid containing the full angolosamine biosynthesis gene cassette under the control of the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>), a hygromycin-resistant gene (<italic toggle="yes">hyg</italic>), and <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> (Fig. 2).

The construction was done as follows: pIB023 was cut with PacI and XbaI, the 4428-bp plasmid backbone fragment (<italic toggle="yes">bla</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tsr</italic>, and the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic> promoter) was purified, and the ends were then filled in with DNA polymerase I, large (Klenow) fragment to generate blunt ends for ligation. <sentence_start/>This blunt ended fragment was then self-ligated using Quick Ligase Enzyme (NEB) to produce pBF27A.

The <italic toggle="yes">hyg</italic> gene encoding hygromycin B phosphotransferase was amplified from plasmid pSMT3-M using the primers PBF27NA-for and PBF27NA-rev and inserted by In-Fusion cloning into pBF27A cut with SspI to form plasmid pBF27B. ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> locus and <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> were fused by overlap extension PCR; two amplified fragments were prepared using pSET152 as a template and primers PBF27NB-for/PBF27NB-rev and pIB773 as a template and the primers PBF27NC-for/PBF27NC-rev, and the final fused product was obtained using the primers PBF27NC-for/PBF27NB-rev. <sentence_start/>The fragment containing ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> (2,410 bp) was inserted into pBF27B cut with SpeI by In-Fusion cloning to produce plasmid pBF27C. <sentence_start/>Finally, the fragment encoding <italic toggle="yes">hyg</italic> ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">oriT</italic> was amplified by PCR using the primers PBF27ND-for and PBF27ND-rev and the template pBF27C and inserted using In-Fusion cloning into the SpeI-cut plasmid constructed by Schell et al. encoding the angolosamine biosynthesis cassette (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>), thus generating plasmid pBF27N (Fig. 2).

pBF27N2 (see Fig. S2 in the supplemental material) encodes the <italic toggle="yes">eryF</italic> gene in addition to the angolosamine biosynthesis cassette. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">eryF</italic> gene was amplified from S. erythraea BIOT-0666 genomic DNA using the primer pair PBF27N2-for/PBF27N2-rev and inserted into pBF27N and pBF28N cut with SpeI by In-Fusion cloning to form plasmid pBF27N2.
Production and analysis of 6-dEB.

Five Streptomyces strains were used for 6-dEB production: S. coelicolor J1929, S. coelicolor M512, S. lividans TK24, S. coelicolor M1152, and S. coelicolor M1154. <sentence_start/>Each strain received either pBF20, pBF22, and pBF24 expressing the <italic toggle="yes">eryA</italic> genes from the <italic toggle="yes">actII-orf4/actI</italic>p activator/promoter or pBF21, pBF23, and pBF25 in which <italic toggle="yes">actII-orf4/actI</italic>p was exchanged for the native <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>p promoter. <sentence_start/>For each strain, the three plasmids were introduced sequentially by conjugation from E. coli. <sentence_start/>After introduction of the <italic toggle="yes">eryA</italic> genes into the host strains, 10<sup>6</sup> spores from three independent lines for each strain were cultured with antibiotics in 25 ml of EVL medium (corn steep solids, 15 g/liter; sucrose, 30 g/liter; ammonium sulfate, 4 g/liter; CaCO<sub>3</sub> 6 g/liter) as seed culture medium for 3 days at 30°C, and then 1 ml of inoculum was transferred to 25 ml of fermentation medium (soy bean flour, 36 g/liter; corn starch, 36 g/liter; ammonium sulfate, 2.4 g/liter; CaCO<sub>3</sub>, 7.2 g/liter; soybean oil, 5 g/liter) fed with 1.2 ml of 40% glucose and 0.2 ml of propan-1-ol at 30°C for 6 days without added antibiotics. <sentence_start/>Triplicate samples (0.75 ml) were withdrawn from each flask and added to ethyl acetate-0.1% NH<sub>3</sub> (0.75 ml), followed by shaking (15 min). <sentence_start/>After centrifugation at 13,000 rpm for 20 min, the organic solvent fraction was removed, dried, and stored at −20°C.

Dried extract was resuspended in methanol (500 μl), and an aliquot (5 μl) was injected for analysis by high-pressure liquid chromatography (HPLC; Dionex Ultimate 3000) on a reverse-phase halo C<sub>18</sub> column (2.7 μm; 2.1 by 100 mm; flow rate, 0.2 ml/min; 40°C). <sentence_start/>Solvents A (0.1% [vol/vol] formic acid in water) and B (0.1% [vol/vol] formic acid in methanol) were mixed to give 40% B initially and held at 40% B upon injection for 0.5 min, and then a linear gradient applied from 40 to 100% B. <sentence_start/>The solvent was then held at 100% B for 1 min prior to reversion back to 40% B and equilibration for 3.5 min before the next injection. <sentence_start/>6-dEB production was identified by its mass spectrum using electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (Bruker maXis UHR-TOF; capillary voltage, 4,000 V; mass range, 50 to 650 <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic>; positive-ion mode).

For 6-dEB quantification, calibration standards containing a fixed amount of the internal standard, erythronolide B (EB; 100 pmol), and increasing amounts of 6-dEB (0 to 100 pmol) were prepared and analyzed in triplicate in 1-μl injection volumes. <sentence_start/>Both EB and 6-dEB were provided by Isomerase Therapeutics, purified from fermentations with blocked mutants of S. erythraea. <sentence_start/>Extracted ion chromatograms (EICs) corresponding to the sodium ion adducts of the molecular ion of 6-dEB (M<sup>+</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> = 409.2567 <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic>) and the internal standard EB (M<sup>+</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> = 425.2516 <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic>) were plotted with a tolerance of ±0.1 <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> using Compass DataAnalysis (Bruker). <sentence_start/>The peak areas were integrated from the EICs using version 3.0 of the Find algorithm in DataAnalysis with a sensitivity of 50% and absolute intensity threshold of 1,000 counts. <sentence_start/>These peak area values were entered directly into an Excel spreadsheet to calculate peak area ratios between 6-dEB and EB.

In the sample extractions, EB was added as an internal standard. <sentence_start/>EB was prepared (10 mM solution) and then diluted to 15 μM in solvent (dilution of 45 μl in 30 ml of solvent). <sentence_start/>EB-spiked solvent (0.75 containing 11.25 nmol) was added to 0.75 ml of culture, and the total was extracted, dried, and resuspended in 500 μl of methanol. <sentence_start/>Then, 5 μl was used for analysis. <sentence_start/>The ratio of peak areas for the internal standard to 6-dEB for each sample was determined. <sentence_start/>The concentration of 6-dEB in the samples was calculated using the calibration curve and the known amount of internal standard present in the sample (113 pmol of EB).
Production and analysis of erythromycin analogues.

S. coelicolor M512, S. lividans TK24, and S. coelicolor M1152. each containing pBF20, pBF22, and pBF24. were used as recipients for either pBF27N or pBF27N2. <sentence_start/>The seed cultures, fermentation medium, extraction method, and the liquid chromatography-electrospray ionization-mass spectrometry (LC-ESI-MS) were performed as described for the 6-dEB extractions with the following modifications. <sentence_start/>Neither seed nor fermentation media contained antibiotics, and the cultures were fermented for 8 days. <sentence_start/>The Luna C<sub>18</sub> column (3 μm, 2 by 150 mm) was used for HPLC analysis, instead of halo C<sub>18</sub> column (2.7 μm, 2.1 by 100 mm), and roxithromycin (2 μM; Sigma-Aldrich) was added to the organic solvent as an internal standard.
Bioassay of erythromycin analogues.

The antibacterial activity of the erythromycin analogues was evaluated by the agar diffusion method using Micrococcus luteus as the indicator organism (<citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" count="1">37</citation>). <sentence_start/>Briefly, TSB-agar medium was initially poured into petri dishes and left to solidify. <sentence_start/>A second portion of TSB-agar containing 50 μl of a Micrococcus luteus overnight culture (grown 18 h at 30°C in Luria-Bertani medium) was added. <sentence_start/>Aseptically, holes were punched, and then 50 μl of the sample extract was loaded. <sentence_start/>After 48 h of incubation at 30°C, the growth inhibition zones of Micrococcus luteus were measured and compared to those of the appropriate control.

Production of erythromycin analogues in Streptomyces coelicolor.

As our constructs were capable of producing 6-dEB in S. coelicolor, we tested whether we could generate glycosylated derivatives by addition of a fourth plasmid. <sentence_start/>Schell et al. showed that S. erythraea containing the gene cassette encoding <italic toggle="yes">angAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">angAII</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">angMIII</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">spnO</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">ang-ORF14</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">angB</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">angMI</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">tylMII</italic>, expressed from the <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p promoter, could convert exogenously added tylactone to a new compound, 5-<italic toggle="yes">O</italic>-β-<sc>d</sc>-angolosaminyltylactone (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>We therefore constructed an integrating plasmid, pBF27N, based on the ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> locus and encoding the angolomycin biosynthesis gene cassette (Fig. 3), that could be introduced into the Streptomyces strains producing 6-dEB. <sentence_start/>In addition, pBF27N was modified to encode EryF, the hydroxylase required for the production of EB from 6-dEB, thus generating pBF27N2. <sentence_start/>The addition of <italic toggle="yes">eryF</italic> would test whether EB could be produced and provide a second aglycone as a substrate for the heterologous glycosyl transferases encoded in the angolomycin gene cassette, <italic toggle="yes">tylMII/angMIII</italic>.

LC-ESI-MS was used to detect the expected metabolites in extracts from the fermented cultures (Fig. 4 and 5). <sentence_start/>S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N was expected to produce angolosaminyl 6-dEB (<italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 544.5), and the corresponding ion was detected but clearly eluting at two retention times (6.6 and 7.3 min; Fig. 4). <sentence_start/>MS2 analysis of both peaks showed that both contained <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 158.1 consistent with both containing angolosamine. <sentence_start/>We propose that the two retention times for <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 544.5 correspond to <italic toggle="yes">5-O</italic>-angolosaminyl-6-dEB and <italic toggle="yes">3-O</italic>-angolosaminyl-6-dEB. <sentence_start/>No ion corresponding to that expected of <italic toggle="yes">bis-O</italic>-angolosaminyl-6-dEB, suggesting that the single glycosylated product cannot act efficiently as a substrate for attachment of a second angolosaminyl residue. <sentence_start/>Unexpectedly, we observed a very small amount of an ion <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> = 560, a retention time of 5.2 min, which could be angolosaminyl-EB (see below), and this was supported by the MS2 data, which indicated that this ion did indeed contain angolosamine. <sentence_start/>The LC-ESI-MS spectra also indicated the presence of unglycosylated 6-dEB and EB, with peaks at <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 409 and <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 425 (and retention times corresponding to standards for these compounds; Fig. 4). <sentence_start/>A search for the ion corresponding to angolosaminyl 6-dEB (<italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 544.5) in extracts of S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24 without the angolomycin gene cassette showed no peak higher than the baseline noise, indicating that the glycosylation of 6-dEB was dependent on the presence of pBF27N.

S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2 was expected to produce angolosaminyl-EB, with a predicted <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> of 560. <sentence_start/>This ion was observed at three retention times: 5.2 min, 7.01 min, and a very small peak at 7.8 min (Fig. 5). <sentence_start/>MS2 indicated the presence of <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 158.1 from the peak at 5.2 and <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 174.1 from the peak at 7.01 min, suggesting the presence of angolosaminyl-EB and, possibly, mycaminosyl-6-dEB, respectively (Fig. 5). <sentence_start/>Mycaminose only differs from angolosamine by the presence of an additional hydroxyl group, explaining the mass differences observed in the MS analysis (Fig. 1 and 5). <sentence_start/>Intermediates in the production of angolosaminyl-EB were also observed as before, i.e., angolosaminyl-6-dEB isomers were both detected (<italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 544.5; 6.6 and 7.3 min, Fig. 5), and both were shown by MS2 to contain angolosamine. <sentence_start/>A search for <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 560 in extracts of S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24 without the angolomycin gene cassette did show a peak higher than the baseline noise but still 100-fold lower intensity than those attributed to angolosaminyl-EB and the putative mycaminosyl-6-dEB, indicating that these metabolites were dependent on the presence of pBF27N2.

Without purified angolosaminyl-6-dEB or angolosaminyl-EB standards, the yields of the analogues could not be accurately determined, but we used relative signal intensities and the internal standard, roxithromycin, as a guide to estimate the relative amounts of compounds obtained from the fermentations. <sentence_start/>The yield of 6-dEB in the M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N cultures (six replicates) was ∼3 mg/liter, and the angolosaminyl-6-dEB isomers amounted to approximately one-tenth to one-fifth of the yield of 6-dEB. <sentence_start/>The extracts from M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2 (three replicates) contained ∼8 and 3 mg/liter of 6-dEB and EB, respectively. <sentence_start/>The yields of angolosaminyl 6-dEB or angolosaminyl EB were estimated to be ∼3-fold less than those observed for 6-dEB and EB. <sentence_start/>The signal for the putative mycaminosyl-6-dEB was less that one-tenth of that for 6-dEB.

Only traces of <italic toggle="yes">m/z</italic> 544, corresponding to angolosaminyl-6-dEB, were detected in S. coelicolor M512::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N (data not shown). <sentence_start/>Both M512 and S. lividans containing pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N produced 6-dEB, and S. lividans::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2 produced both 6-dEB and EB (data not shown).

Schell et al. also generated a gene cassette (containing <italic toggle="yes">tylAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tylAII</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tylMIII</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tylB1</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tyl1a</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">tylMI</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">tylMII</italic>) for the synthesis and transfer of TDP-mycaminose to aglycone rings in biotransformation experiments (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>The plasmid containing this gene cassette was modified with the ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic> site and hygromycin marker and introduced into strain expressing 6-dEB, but no glycosylated erythromycin analogues were observed in the fermentation extracts.
Plasmid stability in S. coelicolor M1152 producing angolosaminyl-6-dEB angolosaminyl-EB.

To test whether strains containing the four integrating plasmids; pBF20, pBF22, pBF24, and pBF27N were stable in S. coelicolor M1152, spores were grown on Soya Mannitol (SM) agar without antibiotics at 30°C. <sentence_start/>The spores were harvested, and titers were determined on nonselective SM agar and on selective SM agar containing each of the markers present on the four plasmids. <sentence_start/>Since there was no significant difference in the spore counts between all five plates for each strain, we conclude that the plasmid integrations are stable (see Table S1 in the supplemental material). <sentence_start/>As a further test, S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24 was subjected to two rounds of sporulation without selection, and there was no loss of plating efficiency on any of the selective plates.
Antibacterial activity in extracts containing glycosylated 6-dEB and EB.

It is known that unglycosylated macrolides from the erythromycin pathway lack antibiotic activity (<citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" count="1">42</citation>). <sentence_start/>We therefore sought to determine whether the glycosylation of 6-dEB or EB with angolosamine could confer antibiotic activity. <sentence_start/>Extracts from the fermented cultures of S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N and M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2 were dissolved in dimethyl sulfoxide and assayed for the antibacterial activity using a disc diffusion assay. <sentence_start/>The extract from M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2 (Fig. 6A) reliably produced a significantly bigger zone of inhibition than those from both M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N (Fig. 6B) and the plasmid free control extract (Fig. 6C). <sentence_start/>Since both plasmid-containing strains produced mixtures of compounds, including angolosaminyl-EB and angolosaminyl-6-dEB, it was not possible to ascertain the identity of antibiotic itself. <sentence_start/>However, the antibiotic activity might just be a consequence of higher yield of the glycosylated intermediates produced by M1152: pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2 (see above).

DISCUSSION

In this study we set out to demonstrate the utility of using multiplexed integrating vectors to engineer antibiotic pathways for expression and combinatorial biosynthesis in a heterologous host. <sentence_start/>The erythromycin pathway was chosen as an example since it is large, it is well understood, and it still has huge potential for the rational design and expression of analogues. <sentence_start/>The strategy here was to use four orthogonal integrating vectors based on the Streptomyces phage integrases TG1, BT1, SV1 and ϕC31, each with its cognate <italic toggle="yes">attP</italic> site. <sentence_start/>These four integrases use different <italic toggle="yes">attB</italic> sites in S. coelicolor or S. lividans, resulting in the stable integration at different genetic loci (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/microbiolspec.MDNA3-0059-2014" pmid="26350324" count="1">8</citation>). <sentence_start/>The genes encoding <italic toggle="yes">eryAI</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">eryAII</italic>, and <italic toggle="yes">eryAIII</italic> genes were inserted into TG1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>-, SV1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>-, and BT1 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>-containing plasmids, respectively, while tailoring genes were inserted into the ϕC31 <italic toggle="yes">int/attP</italic>-containing plasmid. <sentence_start/>This arrangement provides a useful platform for engineering the PKS enzymes and the tailoring enzymes and facilitates combining the engineered constructs once generated.

The advantage of using integration vectors derived using phage integrases is their stability, postintegration, due to the directional properties of the integrases (<citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1128/microbiolspec.MDNA3-0059-2014" pmid="26350324" count="1">8</citation>, <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/j.1365-2958.2011.07696.x" pmid="21564337" count="1">9</citation>). <sentence_start/>Integrases are able to mediate the integration reaction to generate the prophage but require a second phage-encoded protein, the recombinational directionality factor, or RDF to activate excision. <sentence_start/>We verified here that the integrated plasmids used in our constructs were stable in the absence of antibiotic selection, and we showed also that fermentations for metabolite production could be performed in the absence of selection (Fig. 3 to 5). <sentence_start/>The stability of the integrated plasmids improves upon previous work that has utilized replicating plasmids that have required selection for maintenance (<citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1126/science.8036492" pmid="8036492" count="1">21</citation>, <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1073/pnas.96.21.11740" pmid="10518520" pmcid="PMC18356" count="1">26</citation>). <sentence_start/>A number of novel integration systems are becoming available (G. Taylor, P. Fogg, and M. C. M. Smith, unpublished data) that can add to or replace the ϕC31-, TG1-, ϕBT1-, and SV1-derived systems used here. <sentence_start/>The number of plasmids encoding orthogonal integrases is unlikely to be restrictive in this approach; the upper limit is more likely to be limited by the number of markers available for the selection of exconjugants.

Expression of 6-dEB was robust in the heterologous hosts, with yields varying from ∼1 mg/liter to >10 mg/liter, without any attempt at optimization. <sentence_start/>The <italic toggle="yes">actI</italic>p<italic toggle="yes">/actII-orf4</italic> promoter/activator once again proved that it is reliable for expression of non-native antibiotic pathways in S. coelicolor and S. lividans. <sentence_start/>Building on this expression, we generated strains that had the potential to express novel erythromycin analogues. <sentence_start/>Schell et al. previously constructed gene cassettes for the synthesis of the deoxysugars, <sc>d</sc>-angolosamine and <sc>d</sc>-mycaminose (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>S. erythraea lacking the ability to synthesize the aglycone and deoxysugars but expressing the angolosamine cassette is able to transform exogenously added EB to <italic toggle="yes">3-O-</italic>β-D angolosaminyl-EB (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>). <sentence_start/>We used these cassettes to test whether we could generate angolosaminyl or mycaminosyl derivatives of 6-dEB and EB in the heterologous host Streptomyces, into which the genes for aglycone biosynthesis had also been introduced. <sentence_start/>Two isomers of the expected mass for angolosaminyl-6-dEB were detected, possibly showing that 6-dEB can by glycosylated on either the three- or five-position hydroxyls in the aglycone ring (Fig. 4 and 5). <sentence_start/>We could also detect a mass consistent with angolosaminyl-EB, and it seems highly likely that this corresponds to the 3-<italic toggle="yes">O</italic>-β-<sc>d</sc>-angolosaminyl-EB identified by Schell et al. (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>).

Some unexpected EB and 6-dEB derivatives were detected. <sentence_start/>Plasmids pBF27N and pBF27N2 both contain the angolosamine cassette, but only pBF27N2 encodes EryF, the enzyme that introduces the hydroxyl group at C-6 in 6-dEB to generate EB. <sentence_start/>Despite this, S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N appears to be synthesizing angolosaminyl-EB in addition to angolosaminyl-6-dEB, the expected product (Fig. 4). <sentence_start/>The same two products were also observed from S. coelicolor M1152::pBF20::pBF22::pBF24::pBF27N2, which contains <italic toggle="yes">eryF</italic>, but this strain is producing a different side product whose MS spectra are consistent with mycaminosyl-6-dEB (Fig. 5). <sentence_start/>We cannot at this stage attribute specific host- or plasmid-encoded enzyme activities to these side products.

This angolosamine cassette encodes the <italic toggle="yes">tylMII</italic> glycosyltranferase whose natural activity is to transfer TDP-<sc>d</sc>-mycaminose to the tylactone ring and is activated by the product of <italic toggle="yes">tylMIII</italic> (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ja049967j" pmid="15161264" count="1">43</citation>, <citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nbt0702-713" pmid="12089557" count="1">44</citation>). <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">tylMII</italic> has been shown previously to have a broad range of substrate specificities, both for the activated sugar and for the aglycone (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1365-2958.2000.01856.x" pmid="10792725" count="1">45</citation>). <sentence_start/>We can therefore add the ability to transfer angolosamine to 6-dEB to the range of TylMII activities. <sentence_start/>The glycosylation of 6-dEB and EB, however, was not efficient, since only a fraction of 6-dEB and EB were converted. <sentence_start/>In tylosin biosynthesis, the TylMII glycosyl transferase is normally activated by TylMIII but in pBF27N2, AngMIII, the TylMIII homologue and the activator of AngMII, is used (<citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1039/b807914e" pmid="18802638" count="1">36</citation>, <citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1021/ja049967j" pmid="15161264" count="1">43</citation>). <sentence_start/>It is not known how compatible this pair of proteins (TylMII/AngMIII) are in mediating the transfer of angolosamine to aglycones. <sentence_start/>In short, there are viable avenues to pursue to optimize the <italic toggle="yes">in viv</italic>o glycosylation of the aglycone using novel sugar biosynthesis pathways and matching them with different glycosyltransferases.

Extracts producing a mixture of glycosylated analogues, including angolosaminyl-6-dEB, angolosaminyl-EB, and possibly mycaminosyl-6dEB, had antibiotic activity. <sentence_start/>It is not clear at this stage which of these compounds might have antibiotic activity, and we cannot rule out activation of a cryptic pathway in S. coelicolor (Fig. 6).

Enabling a “plug-and-play” synthetic biology approach to cloning, expression, and modifying antibiotic pathways is a desirable aim, but it is a challenge when the pathways involve many enzymes, including multidomain assembly line proteins such as the PKSs. <sentence_start/>However, using multiplexed integration vectors to divide and distribute different functional parts of the gene clusters is a useful first step, facilitating combinatorial biosynthesis and the optimization of genetic constructs.
